amendments.rule: **A verbless clause with a prepositional predicate takes its supplied copula on the preposition.** Rule 20 supplies the copula from the construction; where the predicate is a prepositional phrase, the copula joins the preposition heading that phrase and the unit heads on the preposition — `בְכַפֵּיהֶם` → *is in their hands*, `בִמְסִלּוֹתָם` → *are in their paths*, `אִתָּנוּ` → *are with us*, `עָלֶיךָ` → *is upon thee*. **A resultative prepositional predicate takes the ASV's supplied result or change frame on the same terms.** The preposition carries the relation that English expresses with the frame: `לְ` → *to be*, *shall be turned into*, *will be unto*, or *shalt become*. This is not rule 20's wholly supplied lexical verb, because removing the English frame removes the preposition's own result relation; any explicit Hebrew subject still takes the English subject pronoun separately. Head the preposition's unit on the English word carrying that relation — *to* in *to be*, *into* in *shall be turned into*, *unto* in *will be unto*, and *become* where no English preposition remains. The ordinary copular case is settled rather than a tie: the corpus reads it this way in 103 units across 39 chapters and never moves the copula onto the object noun instead. It is settled; the note need not hedge it. **A relational verb the ASV writes where a copula would stand goes the same way.** Where a possessive or belonging `לְ` heads the predicate and the ASV renders the clause with a verb of belonging rather than a bare copula — `אֲשֶׁר לַבָּיִת` → *which belonged to the house* — that verb is part of the preposition's own rendering and joins its unit, headed on the English preposition written for it. It is not rule 20's wholly supplied lexical verb: drop the verb and the preposition's relation is what has gone and nothing else, which is the subtraction test rule 43 applies to the same clause written with *had*. Where the ASV does write *had* or *have*, rule 43 governs; where it writes a bare copula, the first sentence of this rule does. **But every sentence above governs a phrase for which the ASV has written an English preposition, and says nothing about one for which it has written none.** Where the ASV spends no word on the preposition's own relation and instead writes that relation inside the following word — a possessive or belonging `לְ` rendered as an English genitive, `לַיהוָה` → *is Jehovah's* — rule 30's one-rendering condition is met: one English word carries both the relation and the lexeme, and the preposition shares that word's unit, headed on the word carrying the lexeme. The construction's copula then joins that one fused unit, exactly as it joins `לִפְנֵי` → *was before* under rule 30, which states that a copula the construction hands to the whole of an expression does not defeat the condition. Test by the subtraction rules 16, 30 and 43 use: drop the copula and ask whether the preposition has lost a rendering of its own or only the clause has lost the tense English writes for it. Where only the clause is diminished, the preposition has no separate English and fuses; where an English preposition of its own remains — *is in their hands* — the first sentence of this rule governs and the copula stays with it. Do not reach for rule 2 to split the fused pair on the ground that the noun or name holds an English word of its own: that reasoning is rule 57's, where each of two nouns holds a word, and here the preposition holds none. The corpus reads `לְ` + the divine name this way in six units across five chapters — *is Jehovah's*, *shall be Jehovah's*, *am Jehovah's*, and a bare *Jehovah's* — and never splits a copula onto the preposition beside a separately aligned name.
amendments.why: LEV.3.16 `כָּל־חֵלֶב לַיהוָה` → *all the fat is Jehovah's* was aligned as *is* on the לְ beside *Jehovah's* on the name. Rule 30 already decides the case — its `לִפְנֵי` → *was before* clause is exactly this shape — but rule 49's 'the copula joins the preposition heading that phrase and the unit heads on the preposition', reinforced by 'the corpus ... never moves the copula onto the object noun instead. It is settled', reads as forbidding the fusion, and that is the sentence the verse pass followed. The over-broad sentence is left in place if the qualification is returned as a new rule, so it is corrected where it stands: the whole rule is returned with its riders intact and a closing paragraph that limits the earlier sentences to a phrase for which an English preposition is written. The corpus carries it — EXO.9.29, EXO.12.11, EXO.12.27, EXO.13.12, ISA.44.5 and 1SA.17.47 all fuse `לְ` + יהוה into one unit headed on *Jehovah's*, and none splits — and nothing in the 103-unit copular precedent contradicts it, since every one of those has an English preposition of its own.

conventions: Sacrificial-term heads, fixed once for the whole chapter by rule 31's subtraction test with the competing head named in each unit's note: אִשֶּׁה -> *an offering made by fire* heads on *fire* (vv. 3, 5, 9, 11, 14, 16), שְׁלָמִים -> *of peace offerings* heads on *peace* (vv. 1, 3, 6, 9), עֹלָה -> *burnt offering* heads on *burnt* (v. 5), אַלְיָה -> *fat tail* heads on *fat* (v. 9). *offering*, *offerings*, *offering* and *tail* are the rejected readings; a later chapter in this ritual vocabulary should follow the same test rather than reopen the four.

A possessive לְ whose relation the ASV writes inside the following word's English shares that word's unit and carries the clause's copula there: LEV.3.16 לַיהוָה -> *is Jehovah's* is one aligned unit headed on *Jehovah's* (rules 30, 49). This matches the chapter's fusion of לִפְנֵי -> *before* (vv. 7, 8, 12, 13) and לְעֻמַּת -> *hard by* (v. 9), and the corpus, which fuses לְ + the divine name in six units across five chapters. Recorded because the verse pass took the split reading and the lemma table showed it only as an ordinary *unto*/*is* difference.

LEV.3.17's prohibition: the ASV's *neither ... nor* is divided between the written לֹא (*neither*) and the waw (*nor*) under rule 14's correlative limit, and that leaves both כֹּל tokens unrepresented, the ASV writing neither an *any* nor an *all* for them. BSB represents both; that is the documented convention difference and not an error. The same כָּל־חֵלֶב וְכָל־דָּם ... לֹא תֹאכֵלוּ formula recurs in Leviticus 7.

Object markers: 27 of the chapter's 28 are unrepresented, the ASV writing the object bare or as a bare pronoun. The exception is LEV.3.7 אֶת -> *for*, where the ASV recasts the marked קָרְבָּנוֹ as a role phrase (*offer a lamb for his oblation*) and the subtraction test leaves only the object relation diminished (rule 16). The single *for* is not a chapter inconsistency, and v. 14's appositional *even* is `added` rather than given to a marker because no marker stands on אִשֶּׁה.

report: Checked all 25 candidate lemma groups and read the 17-verse dump end to end, including the two `added` units and the supplied English (copulas, articles, indefinites, relatives) that the lemma table cannot see because it is keyed by source lemma.

One real split. The chapter fuses a preposition with the word whose English carries its relation in vv. 7, 8, 12, 13 (לִפְנֵי -> *before*) and v. 9 (לְעֻמַּת -> *hard by*), but in v. 16 it splits לַיהוָה, giving *is* to the לְ and *Jehovah’s* to the name. The לְ group shows this only as 'unto x6 / is x1', which reads like an ASV difference; it is not. The ASV writes no English preposition for that לְ at all — its relation stands inside the genitive *Jehovah’s* — and *is* is the construction’s copula, so rule 30’s one-rendering condition is met exactly as it is for לִפְנֵי -> *was before*. Corpus renders לְ + the divine name by an English genitive in six units across five chapters (EXO.9.29, EXO.12.11, EXO.12.27, EXO.13.12, ISA.44.5, 1SA.17.47) and fuses every one, never splitting the copula onto the preposition beside a separately aligned name. LEV.3.16 is patched to one aligned unit [s016,s017] -> [t027,t028], headed on יהוה / *Jehovah’s*.

The other 24 groups are differences the source or the ASV licenses, not splits. מִן -> *of* vs *be of* (v. 1 has the participle predicate, v. 6 a prepositional predicate that carries the copula); אִם -> *or* (second member of the disjunctive pair, v. 1) vs *if* (protasis, v. 12); זֶבַח -> *be a sacrifice* vs *a sacrifice* (the copula follows whichever predicate the clause writes, rules 20 and 49); אֹהֶל -> *of the tent* (rectum of פֶּתַח, v. 2) vs *the tent* (object of the fused לִפְנֵי, vv. 8, 13); בֵּן/אַהֲרֹן -> *Aaron’s sons* vs *the sons of Aaron*; רֵיחַ -> *of a savor* (rectum of אִשֶּׁה, v. 5) vs *a savor* (after a written לְ, v. 16). עַל, אֲשֶׁר, הוּא, וְ, יהוה, כֹּהֵן, תָּמִים, סוּר, חֵלֶב, דָּם and the directive he are ASV wording throughout, each applied one way in every verse.

The chapter’s one represented object marker is LEV.3.7 אֶת -> *for*: the ASV recasts the marked קָרְבָּנוֹ as a role phrase and the subtraction test leaves nothing but the object relation diminished (rule 16; corpus aligns אֵת to *for* in 23 units). The other 27 markers are unrepresented. Both `added` units are right as marked: v. 14’s appositional *even* stands before אִשֶּׁה, on which no marker stands, the clause’s markers standing on הַחֵלֶב and its coordinates (rule 16’s limit), and v. 17’s *that* subordinates a clause whose Hebrew writes no conjunction at all (rule 55).

BSB: no genuine error. The object markers (x6), the יְסִירֶנָּה object suffix the ASV leaves unwritten with the object fronted (x4, rule 22), and the two כֹּל of v. 17 are all documented convention differences. On the last, the ASV writes no *any* and no *all*: its *neither ... nor* goes to the written לֹא and to the waw under rule 14’s correlative limit, which leaves both כֹּל tokens nothing to take. Nothing was changed to improve the comparison rate.

One amendment returned, to rule 49. Its sentence 'the corpus reads it this way in 103 units across 39 chapters and never moves the copula onto the object noun instead. It is settled' is what produced the v. 16 error; it is over-broad for a prepositional predicate the ASV writes with no English preposition. Rewritten in place rather than qualified by a new rule pointing back at it.
